title: Esther 6:12–14
context: Esther 6:12–14 shows the immediate result of the procession. Mordecai returns to the king’s gate, while Haman hurries home in mourning with his head covered. When he tells his wife Zeresh and his friends what happened, his wise men and Zeresh say that if Mordecai is of Jewish descent, Haman will not prevail against him but will surely fall before him. While they are still speaking, the king’s eunuchs arrive to hurry Haman to Esther’s banquet. The narrator does not explain why Haman’s advisers speak this way, and God is not named. Both traditions read the scene as a reversal of fortune that prepares for Haman’s downfall, and they see it as consistent with the wider biblical theme that the proud are brought low (compare Proverbs 16:18), while keeping to what the text itself says.

verses.text: Mordecai came back to the king’s gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and having his head covered.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai returns to the king’s gate, while Haman hurries home mourning with his head covered. Arminians see Mordecai’s humility in returning to his post after being honored, in contrast to Haman’s shame.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the contrast between the two men as central to the story. Both traditions read Haman’s covered head as a sign of grief and humiliation, and they treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him, “If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him, but you will surely fall before him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Haman tells Zeresh and his friends what happened, and they say that if Mordecai is Jewish, Haman will not prevail but will surely fall before him. Arminian readers see even Haman’s advisers sensing that opposing this people is dangerous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the words as an unwitting acknowledgment of the protection over God’s people, though God is not named. Both traditions note that the narrator does not explain why the advisers speak this way, and they avoid overreading it.

verses.text: While they were yet talking with him, the king’s eunuchs came, and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
verses.arminianNotes: While they are still talking, the king’s eunuchs arrive to hurry Haman to Esther’s banquet. Arminians see events moving swiftly beyond Haman’s control, as he is rushed toward the moment of exposure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the timing as part of the story’s providential pattern. Both traditions read the verse as a transition that leads directly into the banquet of chapter 7.
